title: Vayeshev: why so sad today? (Genesis 40:6–7)
hook: in prison, Joseph notices two sad faces and asks why
tomorrow: at the end of two years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph a slave in Egypt, and the LORD was with him. Your line was God goes down with you. What work did you do well, in a place you'd rather not be? Day two hundred five.

Think of the coworker who always says fine. The friend who laughs a little too fast. The kid who comes home and goes straight to their room. Most days, we walk right past. We have our own problems. Joseph has more than his share. Potiphar's wife accused him of something he refused to do, and he's been thrown into prison. Now he's the one looking after the other prisoners, including two of Pharaoh's officials: the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. One morning, he walks in. Today: why so sad today?
screen: `THE ONE WHO ALWAYS SAYS FINE.` → `FALSELY ACCUSED, IN PRISON.` → `ONE MORNING, HE WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: The two officials have each had a dream in the same night. In the morning, the Torah says, Joseph came in, looked at them, and saw that they were troubled. The Hebrew word, zo'afim, means upset, stormy, out of sorts. And Joseph asks them: why do your faces look so sad today? Stop there. Joseph is a prisoner himself. Sold by his brothers, falsely accused, forgotten. He has every reason to be wrapped up in his own misery. Instead he notices two faces. Some readers love the word today in his question. Why so sad today? It means he knew what their faces usually looked like. He'd been paying attention all along, so he could see when something changed. They tell him: we dreamed, and there's nobody to interpret it. And Joseph answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" Tell me, please. The cupbearer tells his dream: a vine, three branches, grapes pressed into Pharaoh's cup. Joseph says: in three days you'll be restored. The baker's dream goes the other way. And all of it happens as Joseph said. This is the hinge of Joseph's whole life. Two years later, that cupbearer will remember a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams, and Joseph will stand before Pharaoh. His rise from the prison to the palace doesn't start with a miracle, or a clever plan. It starts with a question. A prisoner looks at two other prisoners and asks, what's wrong? Teachers have long pointed out how much turns on that one kind question.
screen: `THE CUPBEARER AND THE BAKER.` · `ZO'AFIM: TROUBLED FACES.` · `WHY SO SAD TODAY?` · `INTERPRETATIONS BELONG TO GOD.` · then, large: `NOTICE THE SAD FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask someone how they really are. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the faces you saw yesterday. A family member at breakfast, a coworker, a cashier, a neighbor. Did anyone look different than usual? More tired, quieter, stormier? Pick one of them. Picture yourself asking, gently, you seem a little off today, how are you really? And then just listening. The bell holds the time.
Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion that ends with Joseph in prison, noticing two sad faces and asking why.
Your line: notice the sad face. Today, look closely at one face you see every day, and if it looks different, ask how they really are. Day two hundred five.

screen: `DAY 205 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AT THE END OF TWO YEARS.`

howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts receiving others with a pleasant face and noticing their distress as part of kindness, and Joseph's question in prison is often taught as an example of it.

original.note: Hebrew: troubled, upset, stormy. how the two officials looked that morning.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph was good at dreams.
what it means: his rise began with noticing two sad faces and asking why.
what a scholar hears: zo'afim (Genesis 40:6) is a rare word for stormy distress, used elsewhere of the raging sea (Jonah 1:15).

notes: Genesis 40:7 ('Wherefore look ye so sad to-day?') paraphrased because the exact JPS 1917 wording was not verified.
The trapdoor links zo'afim to Jonah 1:15 (za'po, the sea's raging); the root link (z-'-f) should be confirmed, or the trapdoor simplified.
The reading of 'today' (Joseph knew their usual faces) is a popular homiletic reading, unattributed; confirm.
